PART A
Understand it in 10 minutes

Short part. Big idea: customers and Google check whether your business looks the same — and real — everywhere.

By the end of this part you will know what a listing is, why it matters, and exactly what goes wrong when it is missing or wrong.

1. What a business listing is

A business listing — also called a citation — is one page about your business on a directory or map site. It shows your business name, address and phone number. That short set of details is called your NAP: Name, Address, Phone.

One listing does very little on its own. Fifty listings that all say exactly the same thing are a strong signal.

Google compares the details across the web. When they match everywhere, Google is confident the business is real and the details are correct. When they conflict — an old address on one site, a different phone number on another — Google trusts the business less. And a customer who finds the wrong version may call a dead number or drive to a closed location.

Think of it like this
Your Google Business Profile is your main shop window.
Your listings are fifty smaller signs around town. All of them point to the same shop. All of them carry the same name and phone number.
If half the signs show an old phone number, people stop trusting the signs — and the shop.

2. Why business listings matter

  • Customers find you in more places. Many people search on Yelp, Bing, Apple Maps, Facebook and smaller directories, not only on Google. If you are missing or wrong there, that customer never reaches you.
  • Google trusts consistent businesses. The same name, address and phone on many trusted sites helps Google confirm your Google Business Profile details.
  • Wrong details cost real money. An old phone number, an old address, or a listing marked “closed” sends a ready-to-buy customer to a competitor.
  • Missing listings are easy wins for competitors. If a competitor is listed on 50 sites and you are on 7, they look established everywhere and you look new — or closed.
  • Your social profiles are part of the same picture. A Facebook Page, an Instagram business account and a LinkedIn Page carrying the same name, photo and details tell a customer the business is real and active. Chapter 10 shows you how to add them and link them to your listings.
  • It is work you can check. A listing or a social profile is a live page with a link. Anyone can open it and check the details on it — including you, before you call the work done.
An honest note on ranking:
Listings support your ranking — they do not create it on their own. Your Google Business Profile and your reviews carry much more weight. Anyone who promises that citations alone will put you at number 1 is overselling. What listings do reliably is build trust, fix wrong information, and make sure customers can find and contact you everywhere.

3. Real life: with listings vs without listings

This is the most important chapter in the book. No theory. Just what a customer sees, clicks and feels — first with correct listings everywhere, then without them. The two picture-stories below are normal, everyday moments. The three audit cases after them are real checks from real work, done in November 2026.

Picture this: a customer needs help tonight

A homeowner’s pipe bursts at 8 p.m. She does not know any plumber. She picks up her phone and searches. She will call one of the first businesses that looks real, open and easy to contact. Now watch the same night, two ways.

That night, minute by minuteBusiness WITH correct listingsBusiness WITHOUT them
She searches on her phoneThe business shows up on Google — and also on Yelp, Bing and Apple Maps when she checks there.The business shows on Google only — or not at all. On other apps, there is nothing.
She taps the phone numberEvery page shows the same, current number. The call goes through first time.One page shows an old number. It rings out — or reaches a stranger. She does not try twice.
She checks “are they still open?”Hours match everywhere. One page even says “Open now”. She feels safe to call.One site says CLOSED. Another shows old hours. She is not sure the business still exists.
She looks for the addressSame address (or clear service area) on every page. No confusion.Two different addresses in two different towns. Which one is real? She moves on.
What happens nextShe calls. She books the job. The business never knows how close it came to losing her.She calls the competitor whose details all matched. That job is gone — quietly, with no complaint and no second chance.
The hard truth in that story
A customer lost this way never tells you. There is no bad review and no angry call. The phone simply rings at someone else’s business.

Side by side: the same business, two futures

Check any customer can do in 1 minuteHas correct listings — what they seeHas none / wrong listings — what they see
Search the business name + cityThe same business appears again and again, with the same details.One result, no results, or results that do not agree with each other.
Compare the phone number on 5 sitesOne number, five times. It feels safe to call.Two or three different numbers. It feels risky to call.
Look for reviews and photosListings link back to one real business with photos and hours.Thin, empty or “unclaimed” pages. No photos. No owner in control.
Ask: “Is this business still running?”Yes — clearly. It looks active everywhere.Not sure. One page even says CLOSED. Most people will not gamble on a “not sure”.

Real case 1 — Creative Concrete Company: old details vs fixed listing

Creative Concrete Company is a real family concrete contractor in Palatine, Illinois, working since 1976. When its listings were checked, the business was still showing its OLD details on page after page — while the business itself had moved on. This is the most common problem in this whole book, so read it slowly.

DetailOLD / WRONG — still showing on older listingsCORRECT — what every listing must say
Town and ZIPHoffman Estates, IL 60192 (old address: 3915 Hudson Dr)Palatine, IL 60067 — no street address shown
Phone(847) 359-2309 — the old number(847) 833-3081 — the current number
Yelp pageExists — and marked CLOSED, with the old detailsMust be fixed by the owner — a “closed” label turns customers away even when the business is open
BBB pageExists since 2010 — with the old detailsMust be claimed and corrected — never copied into a second, duplicate page
Google profile at audit timeOld details, no hours and no website link shownCorrect details, hours and website — so a customer can call in one tap

Now the fixed end of the story. A new Brownbook listing was built for this business with the correct details, then claimed — so only the business controls it. It is live here:

Live example — open it and check it yourself:

What “fixed” looks like
Correct town and ZIP (Palatine, IL 60067) • Correct phone • Website link • Opening hours • Full description • Marked “Claimed”.
That one page now tells every customer — and Google — the true story. The lesson: one correct, claimed listing beats ten old, wrong ones.

Real case 2 — the “found, but wrong” trap (a roofer audit pattern)

In one real audit of a roofing business, only 7 of 20 directories had the business at all. It was missing from 8 well-known places, including Yelp, the Better Business Bureau, Yellow Pages, Thumbtack, Houzz, Hotfrog, MerchantCircle and Brownbook. And here is the trap: of the 7 listings that DID exist, 6 had wrong name, address or phone details.

  • Missing is bad. Customers searching on those 8 sites simply never see the business.
  • Wrong is worse. A found listing with a wrong phone number looks like help — and then wastes the customer’s one call.
  • So “I think I’m already listed” is not safety. The only safe check is: found, correct, and claimed — on every site. Chapter 11 shows you how to check.

Real case 3 — invisible, and “half-fixed”

Two more real audit results, in one line each — because both happen every week:

  • Invisible: Fieldwork Studio (Chicago). A check of 20 directories found the business on none of them — 20 out of 20 missing. Outside its own website, it simply did not exist for a customer searching anywhere else.
  • Half-fixed: Debug Pest Control (Smithfield, RI). Found on 12 of 20 directories — but only 2 were fully clean. Its Yellow Pages listing still showed an old, closed head office and old phone numbers, and its Yelp and HomeAdvisor pages showed wrong hours. “Mostly listed” still leaks customers.
What all three cases teach you
1. Search first. Your business may already have pages you did not make — with details you did not choose.
2. Claim and fix what exists. Never add a second copy.
3. Finish all the way. Correct + claimed + live link saved. Half-done is where the harm hides.

4. Before you start: the Master Business Info Sheet

Never type your details from memory. Never copy them from an old listing — old listings are often wrong, as you saw in Chapter 3. Fill in this one sheet first, from your own current records. Then copy from it every single time. This one habit prevents most listing problems.

Your Master Sheet — copy this table and fill it in

FieldWrite it exactly like this
Business nameYour real trading name, spelled one way only
Street addressFull address — or “no street address shown” if you go to the customer
City, state, ZIPExample: Palatine, IL 60067
PhoneOne main number, in one format, used everywhere
WebsiteYour full website address
Business emailAn email you control and will keep
HoursOpening hours for each day
CategoryMain category, plus up to 3–5 services
Description2–4 sentences: what you do, where, since when
Logo and photosLogo file plus 3–5 real photos, ready to upload
Short bio (for social profiles)2–3 sentences: what you do, where, since when — the same bio on every social profile
Social usernamesOne username or handle per platform, as close to your business name as you can get — written down here once chosen
Social profile linksThe live link to each social profile, added here as you finish Chapter 10

A filled example, from real work

So you can see what “done” looks like, here is the top of the Master Sheet for Creative Concrete Company from Chapter 3 — the correct details, the way every new listing must copy them:

FieldFilled in — Creative Concrete Company
Business nameCreative Concrete Company
Street addressNo street address shown (the crew goes to the customer)
City, state, ZIPPalatine, IL 60067
Phone(847) 833-3081
Websitecreativeconcretecompany.com
Description startsFamily concrete contractor, working since 1976…
Rule:
If a detail changes later — a new phone number, a move — you must update it on every listing and every social profile. That is why the tracker in Chapter 12 matters, and why Chapter 13 gives you a short routine for keeping everything correct.

5. The process I follow — and the rules that keep you safe

This is the process this book follows, whether you are building 3 listings or a full set — and it is the same order for the social profiles in Chapter 10. Follow the same order every time. The order is the safety.

Step 1. Audit first. Search for the business on Google and on the main directories. List what already exists: found and correct, found with wrong details, missing, or duplicated.

Step 2. Fix the Master Sheet. Agree on one correct name, address and phone before anything is built. Submit nothing from old, conflicting details.

Step 3. Search and claim before creating. On each site, first check whether the business is already there. If it is, claim and correct that page. Create a new page only when there is truly nothing to claim.

Step 4. Build from the Master Sheet. Same details, same description, same category — plus logo, photos, hours, services, and your social profile links wherever the site allows them.

Step 5. Verify and claim control. Finish the email confirmation, claim buttons and ownership checks, so the listing cannot be changed by strangers.

Step 6. Check the live page. Open the published page like a customer would. Check the name, phone, hours and website link.

Step 7. Save a sheet of live links. One sheet with every listing and social profile, its status and its live link — so all the work can be checked later. Chapter 12 is that sheet.

5 rules that prevent almost every problem

  • Rule 1 — Never create a duplicate. A second page for the same business splits reviews and confuses Google. Always search first.
  • Rule 2 — Never mix old and new details. An old address or an old phone number in even a few listings weakens all of them.
  • Rule 3 — Use an email that will be kept. On some sites, only the account that first created or claimed the profile can edit it later. A throwaway email can lock you out of your own listing.
  • Rule 4 — Stop at owner-only steps. Some sites (for example Yelp or the BBB on some listings) require the business owner to verify by phone or document. When that happens, the owner must do that step. Never work around it, and never submit a claim in the owner’s name without permission.
  • Rule 5 — Skip the paid upgrade unless you want it. Most directories in this book are free. Several offer a paid upgrade during sign-up. The free listing is enough.

6. Any directory, same 8 steps

Almost every directory works the same way. Learn this pattern once, and the three worked examples in Part C will feel familiar and easy.

1. Search the site for your business name and city. If a page exists, claim it — do not create a new one.

2. Register a free account with your business email, and confirm it from the email the site sends you.

3. Start from “Add a business” / “Add Business” and fill the form from your Master Sheet — never from memory.

4. Add the extras the site allows: category, services, hours, website, logo, photos and social profile links.

5. Submit. Then complete any verify or claim step, so you control the page.

6. Open the live published page and check it like a customer.

7. Copy the exact live link into your tracker (Chapter 12), with the date and the login email used.

8. Recheck the link after about 7 days — some sites review or change a listing after it first appears.

Your first 3 listings in one sitting (about 1 hour)
Minutes 0–10: Fill in your Master Sheet (Chapter 4).
Minutes 10–30: Do Brownbook (Chapter 7). Slowly. It teaches you the pattern.
Minutes 30–45: Do Manta (Chapter 8). Notice: here you mostly claim and fix.
Minutes 45–60: Do Hotfrog (Chapter 9), then save all 3 live links in your tracker.
That is enough for day one. Three correct, claimed listings beat twenty rushed ones.

7. Brownbook — step by step

Best first listing. Free, simple, and usually live within minutes after you claim it.

Before you startDetails
Websitebrownbook.net
CostFree. Skip any paid offer — the free listing is enough.
Time neededAbout 15–20 minutes the first time
You needYour Master Sheet + the business email inbox open
You will finish withOne live, claimed listing + its link saved in your tracker

Site screens change from time to time, so a button may sit in a slightly different place. The order below stays the same.

The Brownbook homepage. “Sign in / Register” (top right) is where your account starts. The “+” button adds a business. The two search boxes are where you first check whether your business is already listed.

Step 1 — Create your free account

Go to and choose “Create an account”. Fill in the required fields, tick the required boxes, then click “Create an account”. Use the business email you will keep — you need this same account later to edit the listing.

You should see: A yellow banner asking you to validate (confirm) your account.

Step 2 — Confirm your account by email

Open the email Brownbook sends you and click “Activate Account”. No email after a few minutes? Check your spam folder, then use the “resend” option on the yellow banner.

You should see: The yellow banner is gone. You are logged in and ready.

The Brownbook “Create an Account” form. Fill it in once, carefully — this account owns your listing.

Step 3 — Search first — is your business already there?

Search Brownbook for your business name and city. If a page already exists, open it and use “Claim Listing” / “Is this your business?” — do not add a second copy. Only continue to Step 4 if the search finds nothing.

You should see: Either you found your existing page (claim it), or you found nothing (safe to add it).

If your business was already on Brownbook, it may show as unclaimed in the results, like this listing. Open it and claim that page — do not add a second copy of the business.

Step 4 — Add the business

While logged in, click the “+” at the top right — or open the drop-down under your name and choose “Add a business”.

You should see: The “Add a business” form opens.

Step 5 — Fill the form from your Master Sheet

Work down the form in order: business name, address, city, ZIP, phone, email, website, social links and business tags. Copy each field from your Master Sheet. Fill at least every required field. At the bottom, tick “I’m not a robot” and click the green “Add” button.

You should see: A “Business added” message.

The Brownbook “Add a business” form. Copy — do not re-type from memory. One wrong digit in the phone number undoes the whole point of the listing.

Step 6 — Claim it straight away — do not skip this

On the “Business added” screen, click “Claim this listing for FREE”. Then confirm your full name and tick the box confirming this is your business. Claiming locks the listing, so only you can edit it.

You should see: Your listing is claimed. Brownbook’s own message says a new listing will be live in its search within about 10 minutes.

“Business added” — the real screen after Step 5. Click the green “Claim this listing for FREE” button now, not later. Later is how listings stay unclaimed and editable by strangers.

If this happens…

ProblemDo this
The activation email never arrivesCheck spam first. Then use “resend” on the yellow banner on Brownbook.
Your business is already listedStop adding. Claim the existing page instead (Step 3).
You see a paid offerYou do not need it for this listing. Continue with the free listing.
You typed something wrongLog in, open your business, edit it, save — then re-check the live page.

A finished Brownbook listing, from real work

Here is the real listing from Chapter 3, built with these exact steps: Creative Concrete Company, Palatine, Illinois. Its Brownbook page is live and marked “Claimed”, with the correct city and ZIP (Palatine, IL 60067), the current phone, its website, opening hours and a full description:

Open it and compare it with your own listing: claimed, correct name-address-phone, hours and description. That is what “done” looks like — for every directory, not just this one.

8. Manta — step by step

On Manta, you usually do not start from zero. Manta often already has a page for your business — made automatically from public records, sometimes with old details. Here, claiming and fixing is the normal job.

Before you startDetails
Websitemanta.com
CostFree member and company profile is enough. Paid premium pages are optional extras.
Time neededAbout 10–15 minutes
You needYour Master Sheet + the business email inbox open
You will finish withYour existing Manta page claimed, corrected and completed — under your control

Step 1 — Find your business first

On , search your business name and city. Or start from “Add Business” in the header — it checks for an existing listing as part of the flow. Either way, search before you create anything.

You should see: Manta shows you companies that match, or tells you there is no match.

Step 2 — If Manta finds a match, claim it

When Manta shows companies similar to the one you are adding, click “This is my company” on the correct one. If none of them is yours, click “None of these are my company” and continue adding yours as new.

You should see: You are now claiming the existing page — not making a duplicate.

Manta’s “Is this your company?” screen. It appears when a matching profile already exists. “This is my company” claims the existing page. This one click is the whole lesson of Manta.

Step 3 — Check the details it shows you — slowly

Manta next asks whether the business information looks correct. Compare it with your Master Sheet, line by line. If it matches, confirm it. If anything is old or wrong, choose “Edit Info” and fix it now — before you publish.

You should see: Details on screen match your Master Sheet exactly.

“Thanks for claiming your business on Manta!” Check the name, address and phone on this screen against your Master Sheet. Click “Yes” only if they are exactly right — otherwise use “Edit Info”.

Step 4 — Register, so your fixes are saved and published

Manta asks you to register so your updates are saved and your company page is published. Use an email the business will keep. Manta’s own help pages state that a profile can only be edited later by the same account that first edited it — so never use a temporary email, or someone else’s email, here.

You should see: “Your company page is ready!” — your page is published under your account.

“Your company page is ready!” Register with an email you control to save your updates and publish the page.

Step 5 — Complete the profile in the Business Dashboard

Sign in and open your Business Dashboard. Add the description, photos, website link, services and hours. A profile Manta marks as “claimed” has been checked by the business — exactly the trust signal you want a customer to see.

You should see: A complete, claimed profile — not a thin automatic page.

Manta in one line:
Search → claim the page Manta already made → fix every wrong detail → register with a permanent email → finish the profile in the dashboard.

If this happens…

ProblemDo this
Manta shows a business that is not yoursClick “None of these are my company” and add yours as new.
The details Manta shows are oldChoose “Edit Info” and correct them from your Master Sheet before you confirm.
You already claimed it with a different emailYou must log in with that same account to edit. If you cannot, use Manta’s help/FAQ route — do not create a second profile.
You see paid premium offersSkip them. A free claimed profile is enough for this listing.

9. Hotfrog — step by step

A free profile on a big international directory. One warning first: Hotfrog has a separate site for each country. For a US business, make sure you are on the US site before you type anything.

Before you startDetails
Websitehotfrog.com — check the country flag is set to the United States
CostFree. The paid “AdVantage” upgrade is optional — you do not need it.
Time neededAbout 15 minutes
You needYour Master Sheet + the business email inbox open
You will finish withOne live, verified listing + its link saved in your tracker

Step 1 — Register first

Go to , click “Add Business”, then “Don’t have an Account?”. Type your business email and click “Get started”.

You should see: Hotfrog tells you a confirmation email is on its way.

Step 2 — Confirm your email and set your password

Open Hotfrog’s confirmation email and click its link. Then set your password: at least 8 characters, with letters and numbers. Use a password you save safely — you will need this account to update the listing later.

You should see: Your account is active and you are logged in.

Hotfrog’s sign-up screen. Enter the business email you will keep, click “Get started”, then use the link in Hotfrog’s email to set your password.

The Hotfrog homepage. “Add Business” and “Log in” are at the top right. The flag icon beside them selects your country — for a US business, check it before you start.

Step 3 — Search before creating — claim if it exists

From your account, use “Search Now” to look for your business. If it is already listed, click the yellow “Claim” button next to it. If Hotfrog offers a paid upgrade at this point and you only want the free listing, choose “No thanks, I just want to claim this listing but not upgrade.” Only add a new business (Step 4) when the search finds nothing.

You should see: Either you claimed your existing page, or the search found nothing and it is safe to add.

Searching Hotfrog for an existing business to claim. Same rule as everywhere in this book: claim what exists; add only what is missing.

Step 4 — Add a new business — and pin it on the map

Click “Add a Business”. Type the company name and address exactly as on your Master Sheet, then click “Find address” so Hotfrog places the map pin in the right spot. Check the pin. If it sits on the wrong street, fix the address text and try again.

You should see: Your business appears on the map, in the right place.

Hotfrog’s “Let’s build your basic profile” form. Fill the name and address exactly as on your Master Sheet, then click “Find address”. Tick “Hide address?” only if you go to the customer and do not receive customers at home.

Step 5 — Complete and submit the profile

The form expands so you can add categories, phone, website and the rest of your details — all copied from your Master Sheet. Check the required boxes and click “Submit Profile”.

You should see: Your new page exists. It starts unclaimed — one step left, and it is the important one.

Step 6 — Verify ownership — finish the job

Hotfrog invites you to verify the new page. Click “Verify now”, choose the matching verification option, accept the terms, complete the reCAPTCHA (“I’m not a robot”) check and click “Verify Now”. A verified page is under your control. An unclaimed page can be edited by others.

You should see: The page is verified and yours.

After submitting, Hotfrog shows your new page with a “Verify now” button. Do not leave the page here. Verified = yours. Unclaimed = anyone can touch it.

A finished Hotfrog listing, on desktop and mobile: business name, full contact details, website link, an “About” description and a map. Check yours against your Master Sheet, in this same way, before you save the live link.

If this happens…

ProblemDo this
You are on the wrong country’s siteStop. Use the flag icon at the top to switch to the United States, then start again.
The map pin is in the wrong placeCorrect the address text to match your Master Sheet exactly, then click “Find address” again.
A paid upgrade screen appears while claimingChoose “No thanks, I just want to claim this listing but not upgrade.”
You submitted, but the page says unclaimedThat is normal at first. Finish Step 6 — Verify now — to take control.

10. Adding your social profiles

Listings tell a customer where you are. Social profiles show the business is real, active and run by a real person. Done with the same name, photo and details as your listings, they complete the picture a customer checks before calling.

You do not need every platform. Start with the ones your customers actually use. For most small businesses that is a Facebook Page first, then Instagram, then LinkedIn if your customers are other businesses or professionals.

Why social profiles belong with your listings

  • Customers check them before they call. A customer who finds you on a directory often taps through to Facebook or Instagram to see real photos, recent work and whether the business still looks active.
  • Matching details build trust. The same business name, logo, phone number, hours and website on your social profiles and your listings tell one clear story. Different details tell the opposite story — the harm you saw in Chapter 3.
  • They link everything together. Your Google Business Profile can show links to your social profiles, many directories have a field for social links, and your social profiles link back to your website. Each one confirms the others.
  • They give customers another way to reach you. Many customers prefer to send a message on Facebook or Instagram instead of calling. A profile with correct contact details makes that message possible.
A business profile is not a personal profile
Facebook: the business gets a Page. You create and manage the Page from your real personal account, but the Page is the business's public face — customers follow the Page, not your personal profile.
Instagram: the business gets a professional account, set to Business. It is a setting on the account itself — you switch an existing account, you do not need a second app or a second phone.
LinkedIn: the business gets a Page, separate from your personal LinkedIn profile. The personal profile creates and manages the Page.
Never run a business from a fake or duplicate personal account, and never hand a business's accounts to a login the owner does not control.
Before you startDetails
Platforms in this chapterFacebook Page, Instagram (Business), LinkedIn Page — plus where to add the links: Google Business Profile, directories and your website
Time neededAbout 15–20 minutes per platform the first time
You needYour Master Sheet (Chapter 4) + your short bio, logo, a cover photo and 3–5 real photos, ready to upload
You will finish withBusiness social profiles with the same name, photo and details as your listings — linked from Google and saved in your tracker (Chapter 12)

The pattern — the same 7 steps on every platform

1. Search the platform for your business name first. If a Page or profile already exists, claim it or request access to it — do not create a second one.

2. Create or switch the account using a login the business owner controls, with the business email from your Master Sheet.

3. Use the exact business name. Choose a username or handle as close to that name as the platform allows, and write it on your Master Sheet.

4. Add the logo as the profile picture and a real photo of your work or premises as the cover or header image.

5. Copy in your bio, category, phone, address or service area, hours and website from your Master Sheet — never from memory, never from an old profile.

6. Link everything: website on the profile, social links on your Google Business Profile and directories, and Facebook and Instagram connected to each other.

7. Save the live profile link in your tracker (Chapter 12). Where the platform allows it, add a second trusted person as admin, and turn on the account's two-step sign-in protection.

Facebook — create the business Page

A Facebook Page is free to create, and only an official representative of the business should create it. Menu names change from time to time — if your screen words things slightly differently, follow the same order.

Step 1 — Search first

Log in to Facebook and search your business name and city. If a Page for the business already exists, open it. If it is yours to run, use the options on that Page to take or request control of it. Only create a new Page when there is truly no Page for the business.

You should see: Either you found the existing Page, or you confirmed there is none.

Step 2 — Create the Page

On a computer, click “Pages” on the left, then “Create Page”. Choose “Public Page”, then enter your business name exactly as on your Master Sheet and choose the category that best matches what you do. Add your short bio if Facebook asks for it, then click “Create Page”.

You should see: Your Page exists, with the right name and category.

Step 3 — Complete it like a listing

Add the logo as the profile picture and a real photo as the cover photo. Then add your contact details from your Master Sheet: phone, website, email, address or service area, and hours. Add an action button if Facebook offers one — for example Call or Send message — and point it at your real phone number or inbox.

You should see: A customer opening the Page sees the same name, phone, hours and website as on your listings.

Step 4 — Keep control of it

The business owner should hold full control of the Page. If Facebook offers to connect your Instagram account, you can do it now or later (Step 4 of the Instagram section below). Save the Page's live link in your tracker.

You should see: The Page is published, the owner controls it, and its link is saved.

Instagram — set up a Business account

Step 1 — Start from an account the business controls

If the business already has an Instagram account, use that one — check first that it is not a duplicate of another account for the same business. If there is no account, create one with the business email from your Master Sheet and a username close to the business name.

You should see: You are logged in to the one Instagram account the business will use.

Step 2 — Switch it to a professional Business account

Open your profile and tap the menu button at the top right (Settings and activity). Under “For professionals”, tap “Account type and tools”, then “Switch to professional account”. Choose the category that best describes what you do, and when Instagram asks, choose “Business” (not Creator — Business is the type made for retailers, local businesses, brands and service providers). Add your business contact details, or skip that screen and add them in the profile settings right after.

You should see: Your profile now shows as a Business account, with a professional dashboard.

One change to know before you switch:
A professional account cannot be set to private. If the account was private, switching makes it public — which is what a business account needs to be, so customers can find it.

Step 3 — Make it match your Master Sheet

Set the profile picture to the same logo as Facebook. Put the business name in the Name field, keep the username close to the business name, and paste your short bio. Add your website link, and check the contact options show the same phone and email as your listings.

You should see: Instagram, Facebook and your listings now show the same name, photo, bio and contact details.

Step 4 — Connect it to your Facebook Page

When Instagram offers to log in to Facebook and connect a Page, connect the business Page you made above — or tap Skip and connect later from the Page settings or Meta Business Suite. Connecting them lets you manage both from one place and reply to messages together.

You should see: Both Meta profiles are connected under the business's own accounts.

LinkedIn — create the business Page

Skip this section if your customers are only local homeowners and never use LinkedIn — Facebook and Instagram matter more for you. Do it if you sell to other businesses, or if the owner's professional reputation brings in work.

Step 1 — Check what LinkedIn needs first

A LinkedIn Page is created from a personal LinkedIn profile, and the person who creates it becomes the Page's super admin — the owner should be that person, or add themselves as admin straight after. LinkedIn may not let a brand-new profile create a Page straight away: the profile needs to be at least a day old and have more than one connection. If the button will not work, wait, add a few real connections, and use a computer.

You should see: You are logged in to a personal profile that is allowed to create a Page.

Step 2 — Create the Page on a computer

Creating a Page is not supported in the LinkedIn Android app, so use a computer (or an iPhone or iPad). Click the “For Business” icon at the top right, scroll down and click “Create a Company Page”, then choose the Page type for a company.

You should see: The Page identity form opens.

Step 3 — Fill in the Page identity

Enter the business name, and check the public URL LinkedIn suggests — it looks like , in lowercase. Add your website, industry and company size, upload the logo, and write a short tagline: what you do and who for, in one line, using the same words as your bio. Tick the box confirming you have the right to act on behalf of the business, then click “Create page”. Only tick that box if it is true.

You should see: Your LinkedIn Page is live. LinkedIn itself notes that Pages with complete information get more views than incomplete ones — so finish Step 4.

Step 4 — Complete the About section

Open the Page and complete the overview with the same description as your Master Sheet, plus your phone, website and service area or location. Add a second trusted admin if the Page allows it, and save the Page's live link in your tracker.

You should see: A complete Page that matches your listings and your other social profiles.

The owner's own profiles (optional, but powerful)

Customers also check the person behind the business — especially for trades and services, where the owner is the brand. If the owner is willing, set up or tidy the owner's personal profiles the same careful way: the owner's real name, the same clear photo, and the same one-line bio on each one (for example LinkedIn, a personal Facebook profile, Instagram, X, About.me or Crunchbase), each linking to the business website or business Page. This is the owner's choice and needs the owner's permission and photo — never create a profile in someone else's name without it. Business profiles come first; owner profiles are the extra layer, not a replacement.

Now link your socials to Google and your listings

Finished profiles that nothing links to are only half done. This last job takes a few minutes per profile and joins the whole picture up.

Step 1 — Add the links to your Google Business Profile

Open your Business Profile and choose “Edit profile”, then “Contact”. Next to “Social profiles”, choose Edit. For each platform, select it from the list, paste the full link to your profile (the profile's own address, not a link to one post), and choose “Add social profile” to add the next one. You can add one link per platform. Then Save.

You should see: A customer who finds you on Google can now tap straight through to your Facebook, Instagram or LinkedIn.

  • If you do not see “Social profiles”: Google says this feature is only available in some regions for now. Skip it, note it in your tracker, and check again in a few months — nothing else in this chapter depends on it.
  • Check links Google added itself: Google can sometimes add social links to a profile automatically. Open your profile like a customer and check every social link shown is yours and correct. Fix or remove any that are not.

Step 2 — Add the links to your directories and website

Go back to the listings you built in Chapters 7–9. Wherever a form has a social links or website field — the Brownbook form has one — paste the same profile links. Then ask whoever runs your website to add the same social links or icons to the website, pointing at the profiles. Every link must point at the real, finished profile — never at an empty or duplicate one.

You should see: Listings, Google, website and social profiles all point at each other, with the same details everywhere.

If this happens…

ProblemDo this
The username you want is takenAdd your city or your service to the handle (for example your name + city). Do not change the business name itself to something different — the name must stay the same everywhere.
A Page or profile already exists, made by someone elseDo not create a second one. Use that platform's own access or claim process to request control, with proof the business is yours. If the platform says only the owner can do a step, the owner does that step.
LinkedIn will not let you create a PageUse a computer (not the Android app), make sure the personal profile is not brand new and has more than one connection, and confirm you are listed as working at the business.
An old profile shows an old phone or addressEdit that profile from your Master Sheet before you link to it from anywhere. Linking to a wrong profile spreads the wrong details faster.
You are offered paid boosts or ads while setting upSkip them. Setting up and completing the profiles in this chapter needs no payment.

PART D
Finish strong and keep it correct

A listing is not done when you press Submit. It is done when a customer can open it, trust it, and call you — and you can prove it with a saved live link.

This part shows you how to check finished work, the mistakes that undo it, and how to keep all of it correct over time.

11. After a listing goes live

Do these 4 checks for every listing and every social profile, every time. They take two minutes and catch almost every error while it is still easy to fix.

1. Open the live page in a private / incognito window — the way a customer who is not logged in will see it.

2. Check the name, address, phone, hours and website link against your Master Sheet, letter by letter and digit by digit.

3. Copy the exact live web address (URL) into your tracker (Chapter 12), with today’s date and the login email you used.

4. Recheck the same link after about 7 days — and again whenever your phone, address or hours change.

Why the 7-day recheck matters
Some sites review a new listing after it first appears. Details can be changed, shortened or held back. A link you checked on day 1 and never again can quietly become a wrong listing — the exact harm you saw in Chapter 3.

Common mistakes that undo the work

MistakeWhat happensDo this instead
Creating a second listingReviews and trust split across two pagesSearch first; claim the existing page
Copying details from an old listingAn old phone or address spreads to 50 sitesAlways copy from the Master Sheet
A slightly different name or phone formatGoogle sees conflicting businessesOne spelling, one number, everywhere
Registering with a throwaway emailYou are locked out of your own profileUse a permanent business email
Stopping at “submitted”An unclaimed page others can editAlways finish the claim / verify step
Not saving the live linkNo proof, and no easy way to update it laterRecord every link in the tracker
Fixing one site and forgetting the restOld details keep leaking customersWhen one detail changes, update every row in the tracker

13. Keeping it correct — your ongoing routine

A listing or a social profile is not a one-time job. Businesses move, phone numbers change, hours change at holidays, and sites sometimes edit, shorten or re-check a listing after it appears. A correct set of profiles slowly becomes a wrong set if nobody looks at it again — and wrong details are the harm this whole book exists to prevent.

The routine below is short on purpose. It is the minimum that keeps everything in Chapters 7–10 true over time.

WhenWhat to do
Once a month (about 30 minutes)Open 5 or 6 rows of your tracker (Chapter 12) — a different set each month — and check each live link like a customer: name, phone, address or service area, hours, website. Open your Facebook, Instagram and LinkedIn profiles the same way. Fix anything that has drifted, on the spot.
Whenever anything changesUpdate your Master Sheet first (Chapter 4). Then work down the tracker and update that one detail on every listing and every social profile — the same week, not “later”. One new phone number left old on half your profiles is the exact trap from Chapter 3.
Every few monthsSearch your business name + city on Google, the way a stranger would. Look for duplicates, pages you did not make, and details that do not match. Claim and fix what you find (Chapters 5–10 show you how), and add anything new to the tracker.
When someone leaves the businessRemove their admin access to your Pages and accounts the same week, and change shared passwords. Your profiles must always be controlled by people the owner trusts now — not by whoever set them up years ago.
What this book covered — and what it did not
Covered: what listings are, why correct details everywhere matter, real examples of the harm when they are missing or wrong, the Master Sheet, a safe process, and full steps for Brownbook, Manta, Hotfrog and your social profiles — plus how to check and keep it all correct.
Not covered: paid advertising, asking for and replying to reviews in detail, and full search-ranking work. That is deliberate. Listings and social profiles build trust and make sure customers can find and contact you — they support your ranking, but on their own they do not guarantee a top position, and this book does not promise one.
If you have worked through Part C, you now have the complete method. Keep the tracker, keep the routine, and your profiles will keep telling the same true story everywhere.
